title: Deterministic frequency summaries at Count-Min space
formal:
Can deterministic one-pass frequency estimation over arbitrary insertion-and-deletion streams match the inverse-accuracy dependence and logarithmic bit-space bound of Count-Min?

Precisely, does there exist one deterministic streaming algorithm and an absolute constant \(C>0\) with the following guarantee? For every pair of integers \(n\ge2\) and \(k\ge2\), initialize a zero vector in \(\mathbb Z^n\) and read any finite stream of updates \((i,\Delta)\in[n]\times\{-1,+1\}\). Write \(f\) for the final vector and
\[M(\sigma)=\max\!\left\{1,\max_{\tau\text{ a prefix of }\sigma}\|f(\tau)\|_\infty\right\}.\]
The retained summary must answer every coordinate query with a rational estimate satisfying
\[|\widehat f_i-f_i|\le\frac1k\|f\|_1\qquad\text{for every }i\in[n],\]
while the algorithm uses at most
\[Ck\left\lceil\log_2\bigl(2n(M(\sigma)+1)\bigr)\right\rceil\]
bits during streaming. The same algorithm must work on streams of arbitrary length and magnitude, without a supplied bound on either. Query processing after the stream may use unrestricted additional workspace and time.

The answer is known to be no. Ganguly’s 2008 lower bound separates deterministic general-stream frequency estimation from the Count-Min space scale. This is a resolved historical question.
why: The question isolates a real cost of removing randomness from compressed frequency information when updates may cancel. Its negative resolution establishes that always-correct summaries need a stronger dependence on accuracy in the general-stream model, making the role of randomness substantive rather than merely an implementation convenience.
status_note: Resolved negatively by Ganguly, CSR 2008, full version published in Dagstuhl Seminar Proceedings 08341, Theorems 1–2. On 16 September 2026 this review checked the full paper’s stream-magnitude definition, total-algorithm requirement, general-automaton reduction and inverse-square-accuracy bit lower bound. The corresponding author-hosted version is explicitly labeled corrected on 6 April 2008; the 2009 follow-up records the first-norm comparison as resolved. The bound excludes the proposed uniform Count-Min-scale space in a growing-accuracy regime. It does not claim tight constant-factor space throughout all parameter values or apply automatically to algorithms with a fixed prior promise on frequency magnitudes. This is a checked published resolution, not a new proof or Lean formalization by the reviewer.

progress.text: Ganguly asks whether deterministic signed-update frequency summaries can match Count-Min’s space bound and conjectures that they cannot.

The corrected full CSR paper proves an \(\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\log M)-O(\log n)\) deterministic bit-space lower bound for total general-stream algorithms, resolving the proposed comparison negatively.
The follow-up explicitly records the first-norm deterministic-versus-randomized separation and turns to other norm normalizations.
Nelson, Nguyẽn and Woodruff give improved deterministic linear-sketch constructions and related lower bounds, refining the already separated deterministic regime.

importance.reason: A fundamental separation between randomized and deterministic streaming summaries for a widely used primitive. The scope reaches general signed-update algorithms, not one data structure, but the precise historical question has a published negative answer and belongs in the inactive archive.

sentences: A signed-update stream changes integer item frequencies through insertions and deletions in arbitrary order.
The historical question asks whether an always-correct deterministic summary can estimate every coordinate with final-first-norm error using Count-Min-scale space.
The model permits arbitrary stream lengths and magnitudes and charges memory in bits.
Ganguly’s 2008 lower bound proves a larger inverse-accuracy dependence for general deterministic stream algorithms.
The original comparison is therefore resolved negatively and the completed record belongs in the inactive archive.

definitions:
A stream is a finite ordered sequence \(\sigma=((i_1,\Delta_1),\ldots,(i_T,\Delta_T))\), where \(i_t\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\Delta_t\in\{-1,+1\}\). The vector after the first \(t\) updates is defined by
\[f_j^{(t)}=\sum_{r=1}^{t}\Delta_r\mathbf1_{i_r=j},\qquad j\in[n].\]
Here \(\mathbf1_{i_r=j}\) is one if the equality holds and zero otherwise; \(f=f^{(T)}\). Negative coordinates are allowed at intermediate times and at the end. Deleting an item that is currently absent is a legal update. The stream order is arbitrary. The empty stream is included.

The norms are \(\|f\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|f_i|\) and \(\|f\|_\infty=\max_i|f_i|\). The error is measured against the final vector’s first norm, which can be much smaller than the total number of updates because insertions and deletions cancel. If the final vector is zero, every returned estimate must be exactly zero. No division by the zero norm is used in the definition.

The input magnitude \(M(\sigma)\) is the largest absolute coordinate value reached by any prefix, with a floor of one for the zero case. It is not the number \(T\) of updates, and it need not be the largest coordinate of the final vector. In particular, an arbitrarily long stream can have small \(M\). The short source page leaves its size symbol unspecified; this card uses the prefix-magnitude definition in §1 of Ganguly’s full 2008 paper. No promise bounds the length, number of cancellations or intermediate frequencies. A different problem with a fixed, preannounced finite range of legal frequencies is not substituted for this total-stream model.

One pass means that the algorithm reads each update once in its given order, retains its internal state, and cannot reread earlier updates. Use a uniform deterministic Turing-machine implementation, with binary encodings of \(n,k\) and the update indices, a one-way input stream, finite control and a binary work tape. The update sign is one bit. There is one finite program for all \(n,k\); no nonuniform advice, free stored table or random seed is available. The parameters are given at initialization and any retained copy is charged to memory. Information stored in counters, addresses and control positions is charged by its binary description length, rather than treating an arbitrarily large integer as one unit of memory.

The streaming-space bound is worst case over all legal input streams and all times during initialization and update processing. For a stream prefix, apply the displayed bound using that prefix’s magnitude. Any unbounded computation between updates must still respect this space bound and finish in finite time. The statement places no update-time restriction. No output is available as external working storage while the stream is being processed.

At the end, the retained state and a queried label \(i\) are passed to a deterministic terminating decoder. The decoder outputs a rational number in finite binary numerator-and-denominator form, with positive denominator. Only information in the retained state and the fixed parameters may describe the processed stream. Decoder workspace and output storage are not charged to streaming space, as in the lower-bound source. Giving the decoder this extra freedom strengthens the negative conclusion. A separate call can be made for each label from the same summary; correctness is required for every label and every stream. Equivalently, it can output the full estimate vector after the stream. There is no probabilistic failure allowance.

Accuracy is parameterized by the integer \(k\), meaning \(\varepsilon=1/k\). This states the source’s asymptotic inverse-accuracy target on a convenient exact input grid. Allowing all rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2]\) instead is equivalent up to constant factors in space: use \(k=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\). The constant \(C\) in the bound is independent of \(n,k,M,T\) and of the stream. Accuracy is not fixed to one constant as \(n\) grows. A guarantee with a constant hidden in big-O that depends on \(k\) would not answer the question.

The comparison fixes Count-Min’s failure probability at a constant for each queried coordinate. In the randomized setting a guarantee for one fixed query is different from simultaneous success for every coordinate; making all queries succeed can introduce an extra logarithmic factor in \(n\). A deterministic correct summary has no such failure event. The target here retains the source’s stated \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(nM))\) bit-space scale, without an additional confidence parameter. The published deterministic lower bound already prevents this scale, and also separates the inverse-accuracy powers after the usual logarithmic amplification.

No linearity, mergeability or order-independence of the internal state is assumed. A linear sketch stores a fixed matrix times the frequency vector; it is only one possible kind of streaming state. An algorithm that works only when every update is positive, or only when all frequencies remain nonnegative, belongs to a restricted input model. The former is the insertion-only model; the latter is often called strict turnstile. Neither restriction is imposed here.

The assertion has quantifier order \(\exists A\;\exists C\;\forall n\ge2\;\forall k\ge2\;\forall\sigma\;\forall i\in[n]\). A refutation must exclude a single uniform algorithm meeting the bound throughout the parameter domain. It need not identify a single finite stream on which every possible algorithm fails.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existence assertion. An affirmative proof would need a uniform, always-correct algorithm with the stated bit-space bound on every general stream and terminating query decoding. A negative proof must cover arbitrary deterministic streaming algorithms with no prior magnitude or length restriction, not only linear sketches or a particular counter scheme. It must quantitatively contradict the uniform \(O(k\log(nM))\) bound while accounting for parameter ranges and bit costs. Ganguly’s published negative result resolves the research question; citing it is not itself a Lean proof. The statement is an asymptotic existence question, so the numerical benchmark tolerance does not replace its error or space requirements. A lower bound that only matches the randomized inverse-accuracy dependence would not suffice.

source_formulation.text: Problem 4 asks whether a deterministic summary for coordinate-frequency estimates under arbitrary signed unit updates can use the same space as Count-Min, and conjectures a negative answer. It motivates the question through heavy hitters and related summary applications. This card retains the frequency-estimation target, spells out its constant-confidence comparison and uses the total-stream magnitude convention of the later paper resolving the question.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the 2006 question; resolved negatively in 2008

context_blocks.text: A frequency summary compresses the cumulative effect of many updates so that individual counts can later be estimated without retaining the original stream. Signed updates make the task sensitive to cancellation: a coordinate estimate must be accurate relative to the mass that remains, rather than to the potentially much larger amount of processed data.

The source contrasts randomized compact summaries with a deterministic construction based on several modular counters. It asks whether the additional dependence on accuracy is unavoidable. Its discussions of heavy hitters, inner products and histograms motivate the same basic summary problem; they are not separate acceptance requirements.

Ganguly proves that a total deterministic stream algorithm needs \(\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\log M)-O(\log n)\) bits in the stated inverse-square-root-to-constant accuracy range. Theorem 1 applies to arbitrary deterministic stream automata and Theorem 2 gives the frequency lower bound. Thus the result is not confined to linear sketches.

The lower-bound range includes accuracies proportional to \(n^{-1/2}\). In that regime the deterministic dependence is of order \(n\log M\), whereas the proposed Count-Min-scale bound has only a square-root dependence on \(n\), apart from its logarithm. This is the quantitative separation required by the source’s question.

The 2009 follow-up explicitly treats the first-norm version as resolved up to logarithmic factors and studies normalization by other norms. Those further variants do not make the original Count-Min-space question open again.

Nelson, Nguyẽn and Woodruff later improve deterministic linear-measurement constructions and study associated recovery guarantees. Their work refines the deterministic landscape; exact logarithmic factors and computational efficiency are more detailed questions than the historical existence target settled here.

The total-stream assumption matters. The 2008 paper explicitly distinguishes algorithms that must work for all possible frequency magnitudes from algorithms designed only for a fixed promised magnitude. Its lower bound must not be imported into a bounded-promise model without a separate argument.
